title: How this site is built and deployed: a private bucket, a strict policy and a deploy that checks itself
summary: pdlab.dev is prerendered pages and a small Preact app in a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront, declared in Terraform and shipped by a workflow that fails unless every page answers 200 afterward.

stat.label: inline scripts on any page, enforced by a test so the content security policy can stay strict

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: A portfolio for platform and automation roles should be hosted the way I would host a real service. It should cost almost nothing, expose as little as possible, and tell me when a deploy did not do what it claimed. It also had to run on AWS, because I wanted the practice and I had credit to spend.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: The site is a Preact single-page app, prerendered to a real HTML file for every route. A Bun build script reads one JSON file per case study and writes every page, so the deployed site has no server or database. The browser fetches a study's page only to swap it in when you open it. The files go to a private S3 bucket with public access blocked and server-side encryption on. Only CloudFront reads the bucket, through an origin access control, and the bucket policy names the one distribution that may do so.

Terraform declares the rest in a module in my infrastructure repository: the distribution, an ACM certificate, a small CloudFront function that turns `/work` into `/work.html`, and a response headers policy. The policy sets a content security policy that allows scripts only from the site itself and the analytics host, forms from nowhere, and framing by no one. It also sets two-year HSTS with preload, no MIME sniffing, a strict referrer policy and a locked-down permissions policy. The distribution forces HTTPS, requires TLS 1.2 or later, speaks HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and uses the cheapest price class. A missing page returns a real 404 with my own error page.

A test keeps that policy honest. The policy has no hash or nonce for inline scripts, so a test fails the build if any page gains one. Other tests read the built HTML for one `h1` per page, Open Graph tags, no cookies or web storage beyond a motion setting, no fonts loaded from a third party, a sitemap and an `llms.txt` that name every study, and the hiring call to action at the end of each study.

Changes to the look go to a `staging` branch first, which a staging copy of the site behind a login builds, so I can review on my phone before a pull request promotes it. Case studies go to `main` by pull request. The deploy workflow runs on every push to `main`. It typechecks, tests and builds, then confirms the AWS key belongs to the deploy-only user before it syncs anything. It refuses to run `--delete` against an empty build. It invalidates the whole distribution and waits for the invalidation to finish. Then it requests the home, work and about pages, `studies.json` and every study the build wrote, retries transient errors, and fails on any answer but 200.

sections.heading: The UI kit
paragraphs: The look comes from toonish-ui, a comic-book component kit I wrote for this site: thin ink outlines, short hard shadows and a gentle lift on hover, in blue, red, yellow and violet on deep navy. It ships design tokens in the W3C format, component CSS that needs no Tailwind, a small script for modals and toggle groups, and self-hosted fonts. [The kit's README lists every component](https://github.com/PeteDio-Labs/toonish-ui).

The kit started inside this repository and moved to [its own public repository](https://github.com/PeteDio-Labs/toonish-ui), with its own tests, changelog and releases. This site installs it from an exact git commit, not from a registry and not from `main`, so a kit change reaches the site only when I move the pin in a pull request. [How the kit is built and tested has its own study](https://pdlab.dev/work/toonish-ui-design-system.html). The kit commits its built files, because Bun does not run a dependency's build scripts, and its CI fails when they are stale. The build copies the kit's fonts and script into the site, so no page loads either from a third party.

sections.heading: What went wrong
paragraphs: I planned to deploy with short-lived GitHub OIDC credentials, so no AWS key would exist. The AWS account sits under an organization policy that denies creating the OIDC provider, and I could not change that. The module now supports both paths. The site uses a deploy-only IAM user whose policy covers one bucket and one distribution, with the key stored in a protected `production` environment and passed to the AWS steps only, never to install or build. Terraform creates the user but never its key, so no secret reaches state. A static key is weaker than OIDC, and I document it as a known trade-off.

The first deploy workflow reported success after uploading files. That proved the upload, not that visitors got pages, and I have been burned by that shape of green check before. The live URL check came after that. It exists because a sync and an invalidation can both succeed while a page is missing.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: Pushing to `main` builds, tests, deploys and checks the live site with no hand step. The hosting plan expects a site this size to cost cents a month, though I have not yet confirmed the figure in Cost Explorer. The module's README records the reasoning for keeping the distribution within CloudFront's free options and lists what I have not yet verified, such as whether the free plan accepts a custom headers policy. The exit plan in the repository covers what to do when the credit ends in April 2027.

The limits are real. The header values come from the Terraform, and the tests cannot see them, because CloudFront sets them. I have not captured a live response for this write-up. Between deploys, a scheduled workflow requests the home, work and about pages, the sitemap, the robots file, the 404 page and four response headers every 30 minutes, and warns before the certificate expires. It does not check each study. The Terraform is applied through a CI job that waits for my approval before it changes anything.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: Put the check where the claim is made. A deploy should end by asking the live site whether it worked, and a security policy should have a test that fails when the code stops matching it.
